#3646. Infinity Nikki fans threaten to boycott game after promotion by Elon Musk's mother, but there may be a genuine reason for her involvement

Infinity Nikki, the free-to-play, cozy, open-world dress-up game, is at the centre of controversy again, though this time not because fans disliked one of the game's updates. Instead, it's because of… Elon Musk's mother.

Some Infinity Nikki fans are planning to boycott the game following the release of the game's latest trailer, which is narrated by Maye Musk. The trailer is for a new update - dubbed Cicia - which adds the ability to drive futuristic hovering cars. The reveal comes days after a widely mocked demonstration of Musk's own Tesla "flying car", which doesn't actually fly.

While some fans are worried Tesla's cars may be coming to the game, many also simply don't want their game associated with Elon Musk and his family.

"If they promote Tesla or mention him in the game I'm 100 percent dropping it," wrote one Reddit user (via The Gamer). "Why would they involve that man in a girly fashion game, and if they wanted a car brand partnership why not a Chinese one??!? Infold is addicted to negative attention I swear."

"If Tesla is somehow involved in the design of the car (or worse, an in-game promotion), then I might have to let go," wrote another person in the same thread. "Please please please be wrong."

Though Maye Musk's involvement might seem random, there may be a good explanation for it. "Here's something that might surprise people who only know her as Elon's mother: Maye Musk is a celebrity in China in her own right," Reddit user BarbieSpeedRacer explained.

"She's a successful model, an author, and a recognisable advertising personality. Her memoir became popular with Chinese readers, and she's appeared in campaigns and promotional events for brands including OPPO, Fila, and JNBY."

Her image as "a woman in her seventies who continues to work as a fashion model" is one that resonates with the game's Chinese audience, apparently, especially "among women interested in fashion, beauty, and lifestyle content".

"A Chinese company makes an advertisement featuring a celebrity popular in China, and an international fandom interprets that decision almost exclusively through the lens of American domestic politics," the post added.

So far, calls for a boycott don't appear to have coalesced into a movement, at least judging by the game's subreddit. Even if Western players were to organise one, it's not likely to hurt Infinity Nikki much, as most of the game's revenue - estimated at more than 80 percent - comes from Chinese players.

In Eurogamer's Infinity Nikki review, Jessica Orr said it advances the genre of open-world gacha games and brings competition to rival developer miHoYo, writing: "The changes in length, combat and progression all feel utterly invigorating compared to other Genshin-likes, and it's why Infinity Nikki feels like it could (and should) be on the same trajectory to shake up the gacha scene just like Genshin Impact did in 2020."

"I'd rather have hundreds of games and full employment than one game no matter how amazing it is."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Game industry legend Warren Spector retired in August, and somewhat ironically he's been more outspoken than ever about the state of the games industry. After blowing up over the closure of BioWare in October, he took a few weeks to think about it and got even more pissed off—and now he's shared some thoughts on the biggest videogame release of all time, Grand Theft Auto 6.

Unlike the BioWare mess, Spector's not angry about GTA 6, but he's clearly ambivalent: His latest missive on LinkedIn opens with a congratulations to the dev team and says, "It looks like it will be a high point of sorts for our medium and our business," which right out of the gate suggests that he's not entirely upbeat about it.

Spector wasted no time getting to the point. "Its billion-dollar development cost and an undoubtedly crazy marketing budget don't represent a business model anyone else can or probably should emulate," he wrote. "That's especially true when thousands of developers are out of work. A billion dollars pays for a lot of games and a lot of salaries.

"Personally I'd rather have hundreds of games and full employment than one game no matter how amazing it is."

At the same time, he said GTA 6 demonstrates the truth of a point he's made previously: "Give a game the time and money to prove its potential (key word, potential) and you have a chance of making something great. Underfund a game or force it out the door before it's ready guaranteed failure no matter how much potential it has."

It's not hard to see that as a reflection on Thick as Thieves, the stealth game released earlier this year by Otherside Entertainment, where Spector served as chief creative officer and creative director prior to his retirement. Initially announced as a PvPvE game, Thick As Thieves was reworked and scaled back prior to its early access release, and eventually just ran out of money, time, and steam.

But it also characterizes the state of the game industry as a whole, where a select crop of proven winners—like GTA 6—from a tiny number of studios are given whatever resources they need to flourish, and everyone else scrabbles for crumbs. Former BioWare stalwart Trick Weekes predicted in September that Electronic Arts would be reduced to "guns and football" following its acquisition by Saudi Arabia's PIF, and so far he doesn't appear to be wrong.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

In that light, Spector's ambivalence, and his conclusion, aren't hard to understand. "Again, congratulations. Ambition and innovation are necessary for the medium to reach its potential," he wrote. "I just hope GTA 6 is the last of its kind even if it's the best we have to offer."

Andy has been gaming on PCs from the very beginning, starting as a youngster with text adventures and primitive action games on a cassette-based TRS80. From there he graduated to the glory days of Sierra Online adventures and Microprose sims, ran a local BBS, learned how to build PCs, and developed a longstanding love of RPGs, immersive sims, and shooters. He began writing videogame news in 2007 for The Escapist and somehow managed to avoid getting fired until 2014, when he joined the storied ranks of PC Gamer. He covers all aspects of the industry, from new game announcements and patch notes to legal disputes, Twitch beefs, esports, and Henry Cavill. Lots of Henry Cavill.

#3644. World of Warcraft: Forever isn't mere nostalgia bait - it's rebuilding the MMO social architecture that Blizzard spent years dismantling

And when I fall in love, will it be (WoW) Forever?

I don't play video games regularly anymore. Not because I've lost interest in them, but because I no longer make the time, the premium on which has seemed to exponentiate with age. I realised, however, in 2019 that I was a kind of sleeper agent: whenever I heard the opening notes of Legends of Azeroth, the original World of Warcraft login screen music, I would feel the reactivation of a latent part of my mind laid down when I was 10 years old. And so, like a form of possession, whenever Blizzard announces a new legacy iteration of the original WoW, no downpayment in time nor money is too great to prevent me from returning.

Here I am, then, at the launch of World of Warcraft: Forever, seven years after Blizzard first revived the original 2004 game with World of Warcraft Classic in 2019. Once more I set foot on Durotar, to spend as much time as I can levelling up a new Orc Warrior before I am forcibly unplugged by either my boss or, more likely, my wife, and so far it's been a welcome return to some of the frictional - but more involving and consequential - socialising that WoW's decades of updates had previously sanded down.

My relationship with Azeroth began in 2007, when I was ten years old. As soon as I inserted the CD-ROM, I knew that I was going to have to vastly increase my timeshare on the family desktop. For the next six years, school attendance, sleep, and quality family time suffered immensely as I battled to balance my new parallel existence as a member of the Orcish Horde.

It's unremarkable now, but the fact that characters created at WoW's launch are now 22 years old and can still be played in the latest iteration of the game would have been almost inconceivable to many developers at the turn of the century. In the late 1990s and early 2000s, the video game industry was overwhelmingly organised around discrete releases expected to have relatively short lives. For most games, commercial success was concentrated in a brief period surrounding their launch, after which sales declined and eventually ceased. WoW's extraordinary success, and exceedingly long half-life, demonstrated the commercial possibilities and durability of a different model: an evolving, immersive digital environment that players paid to inhabit, year after year. Rather than simply purchasing a finished product, players entered a world that would continue to grow around them. New players, after buying the game (and then its subsequent expansions) and paying for a subscription, could begin their adventures in the same world as those who had been there from the beginning, making their way through its ever-expanding geography and history.

The persistence of Azeroth has been the main driver of its abiding allure for me. I have returned to the game time after time, often just to be enveloped in an audiovisual environment that I know so intimately, and which was so formative in my life. But as the WoW universe was continually developed, the game became increasingly unrecognisable from the version I skipped school to play on Windows XP.

What I wanted from the game had also changed. In a turn that would have been completely anathema to my teenage self, I no longer cared about reaching the endgame or having the most competitive character. I stopped caring about the latest raiding content or PvP rankings. Instead, the elements of the game I had once feverishly tried to skip over, like levelling, professions and story, became, ironically, the only parts of the game that I yearned for.

As time unspooled, WoW naturally needed updates to stay fresh. This meant overhauling many of the unwieldy elements of its original design. Much of this was described as 'streamlining' the player experience, making the game less tedious by reducing downtime and, most critically, reliance on other players.

The original Azeroth emulated the real world in ways that few contemporary games do. Firstly, it was openly unbalanced, with some classes vastly stronger than others, some of which were borderline unplayable. Secondly, it required extraordinary amounts of patience and downtime to navigate. Most importantly, though, it required collaboration with others to get the most out of it. In order to access the latest content, players would have to self-organise into specifically composed groups as big as 40 players large, and schedule lengthy chunks of time each week to make progress.

Over time, much of the original social architecture that forced player collaboration was stripped from the game. Adventurers no longer needed to search for and group up with other players from their own server to complete rewarding content. Automated matchmaking systems increasingly did the work for them.

I remember many late nights when I was prevented from doing something quite modest because there were simply not enough players online, or not enough of the right classes. With my ambitions frustrated, I would often have no choice but to log off and try again in the morning. These frustrations were, I only learnt in retrospect, an important byproduct of inhabiting a world that did not exist solely for my benefit. Other people had their own schedules, priorities and ambitions, and my experience of the game depended on those contingencies.

The changes to WoW followed the trajectory of the wider online gaming industry, where players could increasingly be matched instantly with others at any time of day. These were changes that genuinely respected players' time, but the texture and immersion of the game world paid a hefty price. In making the game more convenient, Blizzard had also made it less necessary, and in some respects less possible, to participate in the social world that had once made Azeroth feel so alive.

It became increasingly clear that there was a subset of players, like me, who weren't interested in seeing an old dog learn new tricks, and just wanted to spend time with the old girl we'd raised from a pup. Even if she did walk slowly, and was a bit blind.

As the years went on, many players moved on with their lives, even if they continued to carry some indelible residue of Azeroth with them. Others created unofficial instances of the original game, known as private servers, and relived those infant years with a knowledge of the world that they could scarcely have imagined possessing when they first entered it. As these servers became increasingly popular, Blizzard, originally very reluctant, eventually launched Classic in 2019, an official revival of the game in something approaching its original 2004 form. Since then, legacy versions of WoW have become popular enough to exist alongside the modern game as a major branch of the franchise.

Re-releasing these legacy versions has been a considerable commercial success. But it also exposed a problem with the project of preservation. The original game, because it is so timeworn, has effectively been 'solved.' Players know almost everything about it, including its most obscure idiosyncrasies, and have found ingenious ways of exploiting them. The uncertainty that once made Azeroth feel so vast and mysterious has been replaced by an extraordinary collective expertise. When new content was added to the game, even the best guilds would spend weeks making no progress. During those early years, players at Azeroth's frontiers had to innovate to find creative ways of tackling novel and seemingly intractable problems.

There are clear limits to simulating a turning back of the clock. Players like me slowly realised that we didn't simply want to return to an earlier, simpler period in Azeroth. We wanted something impossible. Like the characters in Eternal Sunshine of the Spotless Mind, we wanted to forget what we already knew so that we might experience our birth in Azeroth for the first time all over again.

WoW: Forever is an attempt to solve this problem. Like Old School RuneScape, Forever's undeniable forerunner and a considerable success in its own right, it is an expanded re-release of the original game that imagines an alternate future for Azeroth: one in which the game continues to evolve without abandoning the original texture and mechanics, and one that preserves the social architecture that made it so enriching in the first place.

As I write this, my Orc Warrior is sitting at a Campfire, a new mechanic that allows players to establish communal campsites and contribute profession-specific items that confer temporary bonuses to themselves and others. To receive a benefit from Campfires, adventurers are forced to sit together, a deliberate attempt from Blizzard to encourage interactions between players. It is too early to tell how effective this socialising mechanism will be in the long run, but nearly everyone in my experience so far has been eager to shoot the breeze together. I have already shared a number of conversations with other players, most of whom are thirty- or forty-somethings on a similar nostalgia quest as me.

I am playing the game on a laptop using a trackpad, caring very little about efficient or optimal progression. Although I suspect a substantial proportion of the player base shares my approach, not everyone has approached the game so casually. At least five players have already reached maximum level, and many others will have meticulously theory-crafted plans designed to skip straight to the endgame. This is a good thing, and the game should be able to support players with different goals. It's important that the game rewards time and effort, but I hope that the modest amount of time I am able to commit will allow me to feel like I am on my own meaningful adventure, and not a weak player who is trailing behind.

Many in the community have come to believe, perhaps wishfully, that Forever might escape the trap of vertical progression, in which each new wave of content supersedes and renders older content redundant. Instead, the promise of horizontal progression, where new content expands the range of meaningful activities and rewards available without continually raising the ceiling of character power, has been latched on to by members of the community, even though Blizzard's messaging in this regard has not been totally clear.

For players like me, the appeal of horizontal progression is that Azeroth might once again become a place to inhabit, rather than a race to finish. I want to be able to wander off, pursue some obscure profession, or spend an evening doing very little of consequence without feeling that the rest of the world has left me behind. I know I don't have the time to commit to the endgame hamster wheel, and whether Forever will produce a gameworld that meaningfully accommodates players with such different ambitions remains to be seen. But for now, at least, it feels good to be home.

Robert Pattinson has had a pretty ridiculous year. Between The Drama, Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey, and the upcoming Dune: Part Three on the 2026 movie schedule, he's been keeping busy. Now, as if playing the Dark Knight wasn't enough, he's officially been cast as the next James Bond. Naturally, the announcement has generated plenty of reactions, but I wasn't expecting Jon Stewart to have one of the funniest takes I've heard so far.

During Monday night's episode of The Daily Show, Stewart addressed the Bond casting while discussing a string of technological disasters and travel disruptions that had made headlines over the weekend. Somehow, he wove them all into an increasingly ridiculous story about how he was supposed to audition for 007. The lengths he went to before revealing that the Twilight franchise breakout star had beaten him to the role had me laughing out loud. Stewart joked:

I was supposed to fly out to a gig. An audition, actually. Kind of a big one. And obviously, delays at the airport. No big deal. I just thought, well, I'll just go by my preferred travel method, Mississippi riverboat.

When your flight gets canceled, logic dictates that the next step is to hop aboard a riverboat. Obviously. Unfortunately for Stewart, his backup transportation wasn't particularly reliable either, and things only got worse when he tried to contact the people running the audition. He continued the bit:

Unfortunately, we also ran into a bit of a... well, it ran into us, but... so I just thought, well, I'll let the production know I was going to be late by sending them an email from my beloved Microsoft Outlook account. And then the... uh... which... it would have been fine, as long as I could still electronically withdraw the money to rent a car, which... long story short, they ended up giving the role to [BLEEP] Robert Pattinson.

I was already laughing at the idea of Stewart missing out on a big role because his riverboat ran into trouble and Microsoft Outlook wasn't cooperating. But he saved his best complaint for last, taking issue with the fact that Pattinson already has another pretty famous character on his résumé. Raising his fist in mock frustration, the longtime late-night host shouted:

Pattinson! You already got Batman. Enough's enough!

I mean, he's got a point. How many iconic characters does one guy need? Here's an actor who has already played Edward Cullen in the Twilight movies, Cedric Diggory in Harry Potter, and Bruce Wayne in The Batman. Now he's adding 007 to the résumé. At this rate, I half expect someone to announce him as the next Superman. Hey, with James Gunn’s recent outing anything is possible.

Of course, Stewart was having fun with the news, and I don't think anybody seriously believes Pattinson should be disqualified from playing Bond because he's already Batman. But I do think it's funny that the actor is becoming the face of another enormous franchise while he's still working on The Batman: Part II.

Pattinson's casting as James Bond was officially announced Monday, following years of speculation about who would replace Daniel Craig. The upcoming 26th Bond movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, who also worked with the Die My Darling actor on Dune: Part Three. While plenty of actors were rumored to be in contention, Pattinson ultimately landed the role. The announcement has already generated strong reactions from fans, which is hardly surprising given how attached people are to the franchise.

Personally, I'm curious to see what he brings to Bond. He's spent years choosing interesting projects and taking roles that don't always seem like the obvious next step for somebody who became famous playing a sparkly vampire. His Batman was a particularly interesting take on Bruce Wayne, and I wouldn't be surprised if he approached 007 with the same willingness to make the character his own. Although now I also kind of want to hear him deliver the famous Bond introduction in his Batman voice.

Robert Pattinson's first James Bond movie doesn't have a release date yet, although production is expected to begin sometime in 2027. Meanwhile, The Batman: Part II is currently scheduled for February 2028.

Personally, I think it would be hilarious if Pattinson's next role was playing Jon Stewart in a biopic. Stranger things have happened in Hollywood, and at this point, Stewart might want to keep an eye on those casting announcements.

In the meantime, you can catch Stewart hosting The Daily Show Mondays at 11 p.m. ET on Comedy Central, with new episodes available to stream the following morning with a Paramount+ subscription.

#3642. You cannot replay missions in GTA 6, but you can use multiple save files, as Rockstar explains how it made missions "harder to fail"

You cannot replay GTA 6 missions again once you've completed them. This might be a shock to some people, since the option to do so was included in Rockstar games as recently as GTA 5, but here once you've made progress in the story, that's it. Our reviewer confirmed this in his 100+ hour playthrough of the title.

You can, of course, use the game's 15 save slots instead - but considering that there will be many, many more missions than there are slots, you're going to have to think about when and where you want to make a record of your progress. By my maths, that means you're going to want to make a new manual save for every 6.6 percent of the game you complete. There is, of course, an auto-save slot, too, that should help you out if you get Busted or Wasted. There will also be key story missions - you will be able to tell when they are, much like you could tell when there was about to be a big heist in GTA 5, a showdown in GTA: San Andreas, or a raid on a gang lord's mansion in GTA: Vice City - that you may want to save before attempting.

It seems, though, that it's going to be a bit harder than in previous games to hit that fail state in GTA 6. "The team embraced more of an open-ended design philosophy on this project," says David Hynd, vice president of technology on GTA 6. "For example, we really wanted to reduce the number of Mission fails for the player experimenting or trying something different. And we wanted to encourage the player to do what felt right to them for their particular play style."

That means that Rockstar, by considering its deployment of standard gameplay mechanics and enemy AI, and re-evaluating how it approached mission and level design, has created "many different ways" for you to approach any given mission in the game. The result? "It's a lot harder to keep Missions as open as possible (especially in a game as large as this), but the freedom and flexibility it allows the player was worth it," says Hynd. He also notes that the team expects players to "learn and reapply" consistent rules in terms of how the world works - and be surprised when they do and don't apply.

In the previous game, you could access any previous mission you'd completed and be able to play it again on a whim. For GTA 5, you'd simply boot up Story Mode, open the pause menu, go to Game > Replay Mission, and pick the mission you want to play. GTA 6's structure is more complicated, though, hence why Rockstar made the decision to make progress this linear.

GTA 6 comes out tomorrow. You can find a breakdown of all the global launch times for GTA 6 at the link, and read our 5-star review of the game here. If you want to, ahem, 'travel to New Zealand' to get ahead of the timezones, it seems the country would be happy to have you.

#3641. Just how detailed is the audio in GTA 6? Well, even convenience store refrigerators "all have their own unique sounds", says Rockstar dev

If you've been online at all today, you'll know that what feels like the entire world is currently fawning over GTA 6. As the reviews dropped, one thing quickly became very clear: this is a game absolutely packed with detail. Our own Chris noted that, thanks to this focus on specific detail and unbelievable nuance, Grand Theft Auto 6 is "the most unbelievable video game world ever made". And it's no accident: this is something Rockstar put a lot of dedicated effort into.

It's been well-established that the studio has gone above and beyond to make this interactive world one of the most richly-developed we've ever seen: Rockstar has told us it "re-engineered" its weather systems to "achieve a sense of scale we haven't felt before," adding hurricanes, rainbows and heavy rain. It simulated and built a complex drug system, allowing Lucia and Jason to partake in drug use "directly from their inventory" and "at any time". But there are still details emerging from the dev team that are blowing my mind. And the most recent byte of information I saw was related to how Rockstar worked with sound.

"Much of the dynamic soundscape is informed by the incredibly detailed art throughout the world," explains Alastair MacGregor, vice president of audio at Rockstar. "One small example is that convenience store refrigerators all have their own unique sounds. In a run-down store, the refrigerators and freezers are loud and sound like they are badly maintained. Their compressor units can be heard mechanically whirring away from years of neglect. As a result, the bottles behind the doors can be heard shaking and the units click on and off more frequently. In an up-market store, the refrigerators are quieter, adding a subtle hum to the environment."

This level of detail is, quite frankly, absurd. It's a testament to granularity Rockstar is willing to go to in making Leonida feel truly lived-in and realistic. And this level of production isn't restricted to internal locations, either. "On the ambient side, we love the contrast between the manicured luxury islands, with the sizzle of crickets and lawn sprinklers backed by birdsong, yacht halyards clanging in the distance, and yard work going on, versus urban areas with the sounds of people living on top of each other - snatches of every genre of music, distant voices, cars peeling out, construction, the omnipresent hum of elderly air conditioners struggling with the humidity," continues MacGregor.

He goes on to say that if you're wandering the streets of Gellhorn - a coastal city in Kelly County on the western side of Leonida - it's acoustically a very different vibe than the high-rise centre of Vice City, where the sound bounces between the buildings. This means that the engine is handling not just the sounds of things as minute as bugs in the grass, but also how that sound travels, and interacts with other physical entities in the world. "We've spent years iterating on reverb technology to make sure that you can feel that - from the pops of cars backfiring to the wash of a helicopter passing by overhead to birds squawking in the trees," concludes MacGregor.

GTA 6 launches tomorrow - Thursday, 19th November - for PS5 and Xbox Series X/S. It's also worth noting that Rockstar has been embroiled in legal action after it was accused of union busting following the firing of over 30 employees. The case's conclusion will be determined this week.

So you've played through the GTA 6 intro, gotten to know Jason and Lucia a bit, and probably been taught how to drive, shoot, and change clothes. You finally reach that moment in an open world game where, for the first time, you're let off the rails to just be.

That's what I want to know, because I suspect we all have a different system or detail that we've been thinking about since the first GTA 6 trailers and leaks—a test we must conduct to determine if "Rockstar really thought of that." I'm talking about hoops shooting, snack eating, or going on a classic GTA rampage.

Sound off in the comments below (there's a button at the top of the page to skip straight to them) to share your night one plans.

I'm gonna punch someone in the face. I swear I'm not usually one to play Rockstar games like a psychopath, but a bit of random crime will answer a question I've had about GTA 6 for months now: Is evading cops actually interesting? Gameplay leaks suggest that Rockstar has implemented a proper stealth suite with threat indicators and search zones. We also learned that law enforcement will be able to identify Jason and Lucia based on what they were wearing and driving while raising a ruckus. That sounds super interesting, and I can't wait to put those systems through their paces.

I'm going shopping! Actually, I'll probably need some cash first. I will do some crime, and then I will go on a lovely shopping spree. Dressing up my digital counterparts is the main reason I play videogames, mostly because it means that, at least for a few hours, I'm not spending real money on real trainers or the high-quality fabrics that I love to drape over myself.

Going for a drive. I'm also a sucker for playing Barbie with my GTA protagonists, but something I'm really looking forward to is jumping in a car and going for a long drive while cycling through Leonida's radio stations. Rockstar always has an excellent ear for music curation, and there's something about speeding down a highway on a rainy night that hits different. With GTA 6's map being Rockstar's biggest yet, there should be a whole lotta asphalt for me to explore.

Walking off into the woods. I shall find the first tree line and B-line towards it. What interests me more than the cars or even the crime is finding out what kind of wildlife will populate the stretches of land in Leonida. Ever since I heard about the wildlife logbook that Jason (and presumably Lucia) has access to I've been planning my nature excursion, someone's going to have to find all those 62 birds and see just how snappy these alligators are. Deadass, I'm going to be like that penguin from Werner Herzog's Encounters at the End of the World: The PCG team explained even if they caught me and brought me back to the city, I would immediately head back for the woods.

Refueling my car. I'm not exactly well known for playing GTA games in a *normal* way (if there is such a thing), like I spent most of GTA 5 riding around the backcountry on a dirtbike listening to the radio, and not much time at all actually committing crimes. While I am curious about Leonida's dirtbiking potential, my first port of call is the gas station. Having to refuel your car in a GTA game is such an alien concept I just want to see how the whole process works. How much does it cost? Is there an animation? Do I have to go into the gas station? I'll drive around a little bit first to empty the tank and then that's where I'm heading. I know, I know, I live for thrills.

Maura Higgins became a quick fan favorite on Dancing with the Stars, but I'm worried she could miss the Season 35 finals. With the semifinals and one vote before the finale, I'm afraid her run on the 2026 TV schedule may be at an end. Now, it seems I may have more reason to be concerned about what lies ahead.

On the heels of a tough Grammy night featuring the "Thong Song," it was clear Higgins' rib injury was more than a storyline for DWTS to play up. Now, per a new rumor from The Sun, Higgins allegedly had to cancel a rehearsal and seek medical attention while preparing for Dancing with the Stars' semifinals. Her rib was reportedly re-injured over the weekend, leaving some questions about how she'll be able to perform during the live episode.

As viewers learned in last week's episode, Higgins didn't break her rib, but the swelling and damage caused so much pain that she briefly considered throwing in the towel. It'd be a shame to see, given just how far she's come since the beginning, but obviously, her health takes priority.

As of late, I've written about how Tatyana Ali and Jan Ravnik's advancement could set up a fan favorite going home instead of them on Semifinals night. Maura Higgins and Mark Ballas were on my shortlist of people who could go home, and honestly, I think it's all going to come down to who gives the best performance.

I Thought I Knew Who I Wanted To Win DWTS Season 35. But One Comment Totally Changed My Opinion

One can never rule out the impact of fans, however, and I do wonder how this rumor could impact their thoughts on whether she should advance. Part of me thinks she could gain sympathy, assuming she wants to keep going, and get the pass to have another week to recover, give it her all, and try to win DWTS on finale night.

Conversely, I could see some viewers deciding it's her time if the performance is weak or if it's evident that she's struggling with an injury. I would see sending her home as more of an act of mercy at that point, rather than putting the pressure on her to drop out of the finale.

All this to say, I'll have all eyes on Maura Higgins as the DWTS semifinals play out. There's so much chatter happening online about who could go home, and this situation is just another layer to consider. I even think there's a possibility that Harry Shum Jr. could miss the finale, which makes the prospect of this episode so much wilder.

Dancing With The Stars airs on ABC and Disney+ on Tuesdays at 8:00 p.m. ET. This is going to be the biggest episode of the season thus far, so make sure to clear that primetime schedule to see what happens!

#3638. Here’s What Gets Added To A GTA Game Right Before Launch

Grand Theft Auto 6GTA 6Rob NelsonRockstar Games

Some big games go gold months before release, meaning theyâre feature-complete and certified to be printed on discs or cartridges for the relevant consoles theyâre coming out on. Take-Two boss Strauss Zelnick waited until a week before Grand Theft Auto 6âs launch to confirm with 100 percent certainty that it wouldnât get another delay. So what sorts of stuff does Rockstar Games tinker with in the final stretch of a years-long development process?

According to head of production Rob Nelson, it can be adding a last-minute piece of music or tinkering with the open-world polish. In a recent interview with Kotaku, he explained that the team begins to âcircle the wagonsâ two to three months out from launch to see what final fixes, improvements, and additions are achievable before the gameâs initial release.Â

The changes need to get progressively smaller, or they risk creating other problems that can cause last-minute trouble. âWhen you go and you’re messing around with systemic stuff, it’s quite scary,â he said. âWhereas if you’re fixing a piece of scripted content on a mission, less scary, because as long as you fix it there, it’s fine.â

Nelson mentioned that the partner mechanics between protagonists Jason and Lucia were something the team did several final passes on to get just right. He said the free-roam mechanic with the two of them together was particularly challenging to finesse.Â

âIt’s like if you’re going around as them together, it has to hold up if you go into a shop together and buy something, you buy something for the partner, or you go into a club and you can dance together or you go in and you pull a gun on somebody, you jack a carâlike, it has to work,â he told Kotaku. âYou have to basically be able to play Grand Theft Auto with a partner, an AI partner.â

This could include small stuff like suddenly exiting a store or hopping out of a car. Whichever character the player isnât controlling in that moment has to respond immediately and in a way that feels natural. Spontaneity can feel liberating, but it can also lead to jank, and Rockstar wanted to avoid the potential messiness that can come from too much unpredictability.Â

Nelson gave an example of when players go into gang compounds. If Jason or Lucia go to choke someone during stealth, the other will try to follow suit. The same goes for pulling out guns and shooting. This complexity can lead the characters to make mistakes in real time, which is supposed to flow into the larger narrative.Â

âIn that moment you have to make a choice, not as a player but as a partner: Am I going to leave them?â Nelson said. âOr I’m going to start shooting this cop, is that going to then fuck with my criminal profiles? And you have all of this stuff that you’re juggling.â He believes even the messiness of a pathing error can be additive to that sort of experience.Â

Aside from polishing free-roam interactions and scripted sequences, the team spent the final months tinkering with GTA 6âs economy, relationship metrics, and criminal profiles, the reputations that drive how the world reacts to Jason and Lucia. No doubt some or all of that will continue to get tweaked in a parade of post-launch patches during the gameâs first year and beyond.Â

#3637. PlayStation has no Game of the Year nominations at The Game Awards for the first time in 11 years

Last night, The Game Awards 2026 nominations were officially announced, and fans immediately noticed the prestigious Game of the Year category - previously won by the likes of Astro Bot, Clair Obscur, and Elden Ring - does not feature a PlayStation-published game this year. It's a rare sight for PlayStation Studios, which has secured a Game of the Year nomination every year since 2015.

PlayStation has published several games this year that might usually be shoe-ins for a Game of the Year nomination. Marvel's Wolverine is the company's highest profile first-party release in 2026, but it's also responsible for this year's Saros, as well as the externally-developed but PlayStation-published Marvel Tōkon: Fighting Souls.

Despite missing out on the Game of the Year slot, however, PlayStation still features in other categories. All three of the aforementioned games are up for various, non-GOTY awards, while Marathon is nominated for Best Multiplayer, and the upcoming God of War Laufey for Most Anticipated. Here's all of PlayStation's 2026 nominations:

And if you're wondering, here are the 13 Game of the Year nominations PlayStation has secured over the last 11 years:

2027's PlayStation slate of games might fare better at next year's The Game Awards, what with a new entry in the often-nominated God of War series in Laufey, and potentially Naughty Dog's Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet.

#3635. GTA 6 breaks the all-time livestream viewer record hours before it's available to play for most of the world

Hours before it's even playable in most of the world, Grand Theft Auto 6 has already broken the record for the most viewers across livestreaming platforms like Twitch.

According to streaming data and analytics website Streams Charts, GTA 6 had amassed 6.38m live viewers across Twitch, YouTube, and Kick at 12:30 UTC today. At that time, the game had been officially available for a few hours in New Zealand, and elsewhere by using a region-switch trick.

The previous record for most live viewers was set by Valorant, Riot Game's popular tactical shooter, during its closed beta in xx. That game brought in 1.74m live viewers, but it's worth noting there was a promotion offering players a chance to access the beta if they watched a stream. Despite having no such incentive, GTA 6 has more than tripled Valorant's record.

Twitch is the largest platform for GTA 6 streams according to Streams Charts, and already the game is the 6th biggest category in Twitch history. It's also expected the figure will increase as GTA 6 launches officially in more regions of the world.

If you'd like to find out when exactly Grand Theft Auto 6 releases for you, check out Eurogamer's GTA 6 launch time guide for an accurate list by country. You can also read the Everything We Know about Grand Theft Auto 6 guide for a full breakdown on all the details ahead of its launch in your region.

#3634. Christine Quinn Talks Divorce, New Love and Her ‘Selling Sunset’ Return

When we sit down to chat with Christine Quinn about her highly anticipated return to Selling Sunset, she’s everything we want her to be and more: whip-smart, gorgeous, funny and ready to spill the tea. She’s also surprisingly — and endearingly — anxious about doing her first big interview in some time. “I’m so sorry,” she tells Us a few questions in. “I’m a little nervous!”

Much has happened during the 38-year-old’s hiatus from the hit Netflix reality series, which follows real estate agents at the Oppenheim Group as they wheel and deal with L.A.’s rich and famous. After leaving the show in 2022 following a five-season run, Quinn split from her husband of four years, entrepreneur Christian Dumontet, in early 2024. Dumontet was arrested in connection with an alleged domestic violence incident involving their son, Christian, and was later arrested again for violating an emergency protective order. That April, he filed for divorce and requested legal custody of Christian. Amid the ordeal, Quinn moved back to her home state of Texas with their son, now 5, to be closer to her parents and sister. Looking back on that period, she tells Us, “I’m so glad I’m safe, and I’m so glad that my son is safe.”

Today, she’s ready for the spotlight again, and superfans couldn’t be more excited. The author of 2022’s How to Be a Boss Bitch is beloved for her no-nonsense attitude, quick wit and over-the-top style, but she insists she’s mellowed out — just a bit. “A lot has changed since viewers last saw me, and I think they’re going to be pleasantly surprised,” Quinn says. “I’ve grown so much. I’m still the same Christine, just a little softer and more vulnerable.”

Ahead of the season 10 premiere (all episodes available December 4 on Netflix), Quinn opens up to Us about where she stands with her Selling Sunset castmates, finding love again and why she insists she’s a lot more down to earth than people realize.

It’s been a while since we’ve seen you on our TV screens. Welcome back! I really never wanted to leave. But mentally, I had to for myself. I had my son, and my marriage was falling apart. It was a lot. Even though it’s [only] been four years, it feels like so long ago. And then when I got back into it, it was like no time had gone by. I’ve always had a special place in my heart for the Oppenheim Group and for real estate. So the timing was right. It felt good. I was thrilled.

What made you decide to return? Obviously a lot happened in my life; I got divorced and had some lessons I needed to learn. [Back when I was filming], I was married to someone who was not supportive, and there was a lot of tension between me and my work and the office. [After] my circumstances changed, I was like, “OK, what do I want? Who am I?” So when I got approached to do the show, I was like, “Absolutely.” I’ve always loved Selling Sunset. It’s my first love, my baby.

Did you have any reservations? Even though it was an obvious yes, it was not easy because I live in Texas, so dropping everything and coming out here for three months was a tough decision. But I knew it was the right one for me and my son. I missed him, but he was here every weekend with me. We wouldn’t go more than four days without being together. But I definitely had reservations. I worked so hard to have peace in my life.

What was it like to film again? I was nervous. I hadn’t met these girls; I didn’t have preexisting relationships with anyone except Heather [Rae El Moussa] and Amanza [Smith]… And there are a lot of big personalities. I was also nervous about getting back in the groove. I was like, “Am I going to be able to balance all of this? Can I handle it?” I don’t know how, but I did!

You’ve talked about being portrayed as the villain. Any concerns about that happening again? It’s hard because people are like, “She’s a villain.” I’m like, “Guys, you know we all have our levels, right?” We’re all villains in our own way. But [show producers] Adam DiVello and Jason [Oppenheim] made me feel comfortable. They were like, “We’re on season 10. It’s not gonna be dark or petty. We want it to be light and fun. Let’s bring that energy back.” That’s what got me because I love to make people laugh. Sure, I love to be a bit of a bitch sometimes, but there’s a balance.

Was anything off-limits for you? I wasn’t sure how much I was going to share about my marriage and my current relationship. But I realized it was best for me to talk about what I’ve been through and what life can be like on the other side. I’m comfortable and confident in who I am now. I really had a problem with vulnerability and talking about relationships and expressing myself. [Now] I just felt like the time was right to be myself and share my story. I think the audience is going to love it.

When you left the show in 2022, you’d fallen out with most castmates. Do you feel responsible for that in any way? It’s always difficult when you’re in an office with all girls. There’s gonna be drama. From day one, I’ve been really honest about my feelings and observations. Not everyone likes it, but I don’t tell a lie. I needed to be myself, and if in the process there was some collateral damage, I hate that that happened.

Looking back, is there anyone you feel you should apologize to? No. I don’t think there’s anything that I would’ve changed other than perhaps my delivery. Sometimes we get heated and we say things that we [don’t mean]. I wish things could’ve come across a little softer.

Does anyone owe you an apology? Everyone! I’m joking, but it is exhausting having the Cassandra complex. It’s just as damaging being too early to a situation. I’ve learned to be like, “Maybe I’ll shut my mouth and let this play out.”

Have you felt vindicated by a specific cast member’s behavior? I was definitely right about Chrishell [Stause]. People’s eyes were opened. I’m like a truffle pig. I can smell a biatch from a mile away.

In June, you said “the trash needed to be taken out” before you returned. Can you elaborate? Some of these girls are just bad leftovers, and if you leave fish out too long, it reeks up your house. It was time. We needed a mix-up. The energy was getting dark and vile, and it wasn’t fun for anyone. That’s what I’ve heard.

Would you have returned if Chrishell were still on the show? [Stause had accused Quinn of planting stories about her allegedly cheating on her ex-husband; Quinn claimed Stause got special treatment on the show and neglected to congratulate her on her pregnancy. Both women deny the other’s accusations.] I never had a problem with Chrishell. I don’t hold grudges. It’s not who I am. The animosity wasn’t from me. I was willing to be in rooms with her. Even though we had disagreements, I could still show up to work. So I wouldn’t have a problem filming with her. Would it be comfortable? Probably not for her. But she’s doing her own thing [now]. She was on for nine seasons. I don’t think she wants to be on the show anymore.

She’s going through her own split from her partner, G Flip. Perhaps you could bond over that common ground. I can bond and relate to anyone who’s going through a breakup. I never met G. I wish [Chrishell] all the best.

You also weren’t on great terms with Heather. Did you know she was coming back when you signed on? I don’t know the timeline, but I knew she was coming back, and I was excited. We need some familiar faces, and regardless of our situation and our relationship, it was a great decision.

Where do you two stand now? Both on our Louboutins, across the street from each other. I’m kidding. I like Heather. We used to be roommates. We have so much history. Of course we argue like sisters and we have our kerfuffles. But at the end of the day, if we didn’t get upset [it would mean] there’s not real love and feelings there.

Why do you think you guys disagree as much as you do? I’ve always been a lone wolf and done my own thing in terms of having opinions and hard conversations. That’s always kind of set me aside, and I do think there are people who feel more comfortable blending in and having a pack. Sometimes people choose comfort over their own identity.

How has she changed since you were last on the show together? She’s exactly the same — in the best way. Heather’s consistent. Maybe she’s a little hotter? She looks hot! But she’s been married a few years now and has a son as well, and we relate to having toddlers.

How are things with Mary Bonnet? The last time I saw Mary was probably right after my divorce. She was really sweet. I’m not sure what the future holds [about Mary coming back to Selling Sunset], but we all have our stuff we’re working on, and who knows? I haven’t talked to her in a while.

And Emma Hernan? [She and Quinn had tension in season 5 after Hernan alleged Quinn offered Hernan’s client $5,000 to work with Quinn instead; Quinn denied the claim.] I didn’t spend much time with Emma, so I never got the chance to know her. The cultural appropriation empanadas is really not how I roll. [Hernan faced backlash over her vegan empanadas line in 2021.] That’s her thing.

Did you guys work things out? We just moved on. When you’re new and you’re on a TV show, you’re like, “Hmm, how can I get creative?” We’ve all been there. The bribery thing [was the biggest lie about me]. I was just like, “No, I didn’t bribe a client.” They prefer me because I’m a more seasoned agent.

How difficult was it to open up about your marriage while filming season 10? It’s no surprise [that was] the hardest topic, and also how long it took me to get back on my feet. I was kicked to the floor with no life raft. I was hesitant [to open up about it], but I’m using it as a way to support women and to be like, “Listen, like, there’s another side. You can get out of this.” That was the most important lesson for me.

Where does the divorce stand now? It’s almost finalized. It took a really long time because he’s out of the country, and he was evading [his] responsibilities.

Do you remember when you knew the marriage wasn’t working? I was in a really dark place after I had my son. I was dealing with work and tension [with] my ex. I did everything I could to try to make it work. I don’t know if things changed [or] the signs were there all along and I didn’t pick up on it. Maybe. It was something that had been coming for a while.

What weren’t viewers seeing about your marriage at the time? Any marriage is hard. I’ve always had a hard time expressing myself, and I never wanted to look like I had a failed marriage. Was I putting on [an act]? Absolutely, sure. I didn’t want to be humiliated. That’s what women do. We just get through things. It’s not good for us. [Quinn tears up.] Sorry, I don’t talk about this stuff, really.

You don’t have to apologize. Do you think it was harder for you to reach out for help because you have such a strong persona? The dichotomy is fascinating. I built an entire brand on how to be a boss bitch — I literally wrote the book on it. I never wanted to admit failure. But the way that I look at it [now], I’m like, “Nothing can break me down.” This can and does happen to so many other women who aren’t strong enough to stand up for themselves.

You previously told Us you received legal papers from Christian while filming House of Villains. That must have been difficult. He served me intentionally when I couldn’t respond. It’s just nasty and unfair. But that’s what divorces are; you’re never divorcing the person you married. The timing was not by accident.

His arrest for domestic violence was in the news. How scary was that experience for you? It was a really, really dark time. I look back on it now… and I think it’s really important for women to know you don’t have to stick it out just to stick it out.

Did you hear from your former costars? Most people reached out, but not everyone. I wasn’t disappointed because I know these girls and nothing shocks me with them. It gets brought up on the show, so you’ll have to [wait and] see [who I’m talking about].

You were going to work on a crypto real estate venture with your ex. What’s happening with that? No clue. I have no update. [Going into business with a romantic partner] is not something I’d do again. It’s risky.

What advice do you have for other women dealing with similar relationship issues? Lean on your close friends and family. That’s why moving back to Texas was so important for me. You have a support group around you, and they’ll do anything for you. You just have to ask. It took a long time for me to admit that I was seeing some red flags and I needed help. There is a light on the other side, and there’s an amazing man waiting for you — I know because I have one.

Tell Us about this lucky guy! [Quinn’s been linked to business exec Thomas McGarrity since early 2025.] He’s great. He’s amazing. He’s everything my first husband wasn’t. [And he has] hair and abs.

Is he on the show? I didn’t know if I wanted to have my relationship on a show again. I’ve been burned by that formula. But I was comfortable, and everything felt right, and you can have a little sneak peek on the show.

What feels different about this relationship? The most important thing is having someone who’s supportive of you and your career. I didn’t have that, and now I do and it feels so good and like anything’s possible. Like, “Oh, wow, I can do this, and I don’t have to tiptoe around it. I don’t have to be scared.” That’s the best part.

Would you get married again? I’m like Elizabeth Taylor. I’ve always wanted to be married, like, 15 times. I’m not out of [my first one] fully yet, but I absolutely could [see myself getting married again]. If you asked me a year ago, I would have said, “No, definitely not.” But yes. I love hope. I’m a Libra. I love love.

What about more kids? Again, never say never. I’ve thought about it. But it depends on the day.

How’s Texas life? I’m a lot more down to earth than people realize. I’m a homebody. I take my son to school every day. I don’t have a nanny. It’s just me. It’s where I’m from and my sister and parents are there, so it feels great. I go back and forth between L.A. and Texas for work. I get the best of both worlds.

What’s your son like? I think at age 5 they really come online. [Christian] is booted up now; he’s conscious and remembers things and gets excited. Halloween was such a fun time, running around and getting candy… He started [Quinn tears up] — I’m sorry, he started kindergarten recently but before that I was able to fly him out here. He was playing Legos in the Oppenheim Group. I was with him constantly, and if I wasn’t, it was for two, three days [apart].

Will viewers see your son this season? I wasn’t able to have him on the show, and that was difficult because he’s the love of my life and I wanted people to see my relationship with him. Maybe soon. We’ll see.

What’s it like being a boy mom? He loves trains and cars and trucks and building things. He’s an engineer. He’s brilliant and so fun. The clothes are easier with a boy! If I had a girl, the outfits would need to be perfect, but I just throw shorts and a shirt on him, and he’s ready to go. He’s very low maintenance. But he’s still my version of casual, right? [Laughs.]

And what are you wearing to school drop-off? Oh, I look deranged. Definitely sweatpants in the morning. I [also] love jeans. I love a tank top. Scrunchie in my hair. That’s my go-to.

How is coparenting with your ex? There’s no coparenting. I’m the only parent. [I have] full custody. I’m a single mom, and it’s literally just me. There’s no financial help or relationship. In a weird way, I’m grateful.

Why? I’ve seen people coparent, and it’s difficult. It’s really hard with the back-and-forth.

What’s been the hardest part of parenting on your own? The questions around “What is a dad?” and “What is a father?” He hears these words, and he hears me call my dad “Dad.” He was asking questions and I didn’t know how to answer them. You’ll see me navigate it in the show.

How did you approach your wardrobe for your return? It was hard because I have tons of clothes and purses and shoes, but I live in Texas, so when it came time to film, I was like, “Oh, I don’t have earrings and shoes and purses and things to pull together.” My stylist and I had to work overtime. It’s an integral part of who I am on the show. Sometimes we’ll all be like, “We’re gonna go to a coffee shop,” and then it’s like, “Just kidding, we’re gonna have a night out.” I’m like, “I don’t have any clothes for that!”

Looking back at your previous seasons, are there any looks you regret? Honestly, no, because even the flops were still kind of fire. [But] me and Jason were at an open house, and I was wearing, like, a white cab driver hat. I was like, “Oh yeah, this is the best idea ever.” It looked like I had a taxi service. I see clips on TikTok now and I’m like, “Oh God, that was really a choice.”

Have you been happy diving back into the L.A. real estate scene? Being back here and seeing these beautiful views and amazing houses, I’m like, “Oh, my God, this is what I fell in love with.” I have clients in Texas, but L.A. is a different market.

What’s the craziest thing you’ve seen during a showing? I had a beautiful listing in Orange County, an $18 million all-white mansion. The woman came, and I’m showing her the garage and all of a sudden, there’s a person in the car. She’s like, “Oh, my God, there’s someone in the car!” And I’m like, “Did my client murder someone?” She was so freaked out she left. When I went back, I was like, “Oh, wait, it’s a mannequin so he can drive through the HOV lane.” I had to go back and say, “That’s not a real person. It’s a mannequin.”

#3633. GTA 6 Finally Explains Why You Can Hear The Police Radio Chatter

If you’ve played any of the mainline Grand Theft Auto games, you’ve likely committed a crime and heard a police radio communication reporting your naughty behavior. It’s been a part of the series since the first game. And yet, Grand Theft Auto 6 is the first game in the series to actually explain how your character can hear this police chatter.

Early on in Grand Theft Auto 6, Jason’s hacker friend and stoner buddy Cal does the character a solid. He grabs his phone and installs a custom, homebrew police radio scanner program. From then on, Jason can hear the police reporting on his actions, crimes, and location, as was the case in (nearly) every previous GTA game. Later on, when GTA 6 lets you free-roam around as Lucia, she, too, has the same police scanner app installed on her phone. The game doesn’t show Cal installing it, so I’ll just assume it happened off-camera.

Now, to be clear, I don’t think Rockstar needed to dedicate any time or effort to explaining how players could hear police radio chatter in GTA. Sure, sometimes I’d think about how it was possible for characters like CJ or Tommy Vercetti to hear the police reporting on their crimes, but then I would just remind myself it’s a video game, and games are filled with stuff that doesn’t make sense. Characters die and then respawn. Protagonists never age. And you can hear the police radio chatter despite not having a scanner. Just usual video game-y nonsense.

Still, I think it’s fun that for GTA 6, Rockstar took the time to explain how Jason and Lucia can hear the police radio chatter. And it also factors into gameplay. Our protagonists know if the police have spotted their car or have reported their clothing. They even mention it during chases as they try to make their escape, so it’s important we understand that the characters, and not just the player, can hear the chatter. In past games, you could just assume it was a gameplay mechanic, and the protagonists didn’t hear the radio messages. Not so in GTA 6.

I guess Rockstar felt like it was finally necessary to provide a grounded explanation for this classic GTA feature.Â I await Rockstar explaining why every state in the GTA universe is an island in Grand Theft Auto 7.Â

Back in August, the public was devastated to learn that actress Hayden Panettiere died at age 36. This was a huge shock, especially considering her brother died just a few years earlier. Fans are still mourning and re-watching her work on projects like Heroes, and plenty of people were surprised when Panettiere's mother Lesley Vogel didn't attend her celebration of life back in September. Now Vogel is speaking out and explaining her absence for the services.

Fans still have questions about Hayden Panettiere's death, and were curious about why her mother wasn't in attendance for the late actress' funeral services. Lesley Vogel recently appeared on Inside Edition, where she explained why she chose to opt out of her daughter's celebration of life. She was quoted saying:

I just didn’t want to rock the boat either; it was probably for the best.

During the interview, she shared that she and Hayden Panettiere drifted away from each other after the Scream actress' relationship with ex Brian Hickerson started picking up. They mother and daughter seemingly had a difficult relationship, some of which was mentioned in the actress' memoir This Is Me: A Reckoning. Still, it was surprising for some that Vogel didn't attend the funeral services.

While appearing in the same interview, Lesley Vogel claimed that she was indeed invited, but didn't think her presence would be helpful during this difficult time. She went on to say:

I knew that some of the people there wanted to believe I was the horrible mother because Hayden was angry and made statements.

Clearly this was a complicated situation, which might explain why Hayden Panettiere's mother ultimately decided not to attend her funeral. She knew there'd be discourse about her either way, but is seemingly at peace with her decision. Inside Edition contacted Brian Hickerson for a comment, but did not hear back from him.

Panettiere's death hit the public hard, largely because she grew up right in front of our eyes, including early roles in projects like Remember the Titans and A Bug's Life. Millennial fans in particular grew up alongside her, and there was a ton of love her work on Ice Princess, Heroes, Nashville, and the Scream movies (the latter of which are streaming with a Paramount+ subscription). Folks were thrilled when she reprised her role as Kirby Reed in Scream VI, with Panettiere thanking fans who "came to her rescue". Clearly she's someone who meant a great deal to her fans, many of whom are still processing her death. As for Lesley Vogel, she's given an explanation for missing her late daughter's funeral.

Hayden Panettiere's legacy lives on through her various acting credits. Heroes is streaming on Netflix, while Nashville is over on Pluto TV. Our thoughts continue to be with her loved ones as they mourn and grapple with the loss.

Following a backlash from casters and esports fans, Embark Studios has taken down a recap video from a recent esports tournament for The Finals that replaced the original casters' voices with AI.

The commentators for the APAC Closed Qualifiers for The Grand Major, the annual championship tournament for Embark's team-based FPS, were human. But, as reported by IGN, a highlight video released by Embark built from clips from the qualifier replaced those casters with audio from the game's AI commentators, Scotty and June.

It did not go over well. "After 4 cycles, open/closed quals, the time, effort, passion and emotion myself @TheeHyperactive and @bluepanda_casts put in," The Finals caster ProtoANZ wrote on X. "We get replaced by two AI casters who even quote us :/ I get they are apart of the game but yikes. Thanks @reachthefinals."

Reposting ProtoANZ's message, Bluepanda added, "For nearly 7 years I've been repeatedly told that my work is valued and appreciated only to then have the same people saying those things turn around and either completely ghost me or tell me they're going in a different direction with talent and that my services aren't needed GG."

Other casters soon weighed in to express support for ProtoANZ and Bluepanda: League of Legends caster Sam "Initialise" Hapgood called it "dystopian," while Jen "LemonKiwi" Pichette described it as "appalling" and said "REAL casters deserve better."

Embark's relationship with AI in game development has always been messy. It recently announced a new "dynamic commentary" feature for The Finals that enables Scotty and June, the game's AI commentators, to call out specific gameplay events and individual player names, and earlier this month it defended the use of AI voices in Arc Raiders, saying it was "too impractical to record every possible version" of in-game items because the voice actors—people who literally make their living reading scripts—"would just go crazy if they had to read all of that."

That has resulted in some dissenting voices in the mix, and a few responses to ProtoANZ's message opined that this was merely a natural and predictable evolution of Embark's approach.

Keep up to date with the most important stories and the best deals, as picked by the PC Gamer team.

In a message posted to X, however, Embark community and competitive operations lead Oscar Lundberg apologized for replacing the casters' voices with AI, saying it was a "mistake."

"We intended for Scotty and June to help bring more casual interest into The Finals esports ahead of TGM. That was the goal, but the work of our talent deserved to be included and highlighted, and it wasn’t," Lundberg wrote. "The video is down and won’t return in this form. The AMER and EMEA recaps planned in the same format won’t go out as planned either, and we’re rethinking all three."

Embark expressed similar sentiments in a statement shared with IGN, saying that replacing caster voices with AI "wasn't the right call" and expressing gratitude for the "candid feedback."

But that didn't fly with the casters at the heart of the matter. "Embark saw no issue with this until they received overwhelming global backlash and even then their response was essentially, 'Whoopsie, we didn't think people would mind'," Bluepanda told the site. "It says to me that they're not really sorry at all. I'm done with the game and esports as a whole at this stage, the effort we put in and the amount of bullshit we have to deal with, especially in OCE, just isn't worth it anymore."

Calling the situation "a shit show," ProtoANZ called for the creation of an esports talent union to protect commentary and production teams: "We'll turn around and say, 'We're not doing this until people send us contracts that essentially ban the use of our voices in generative AI'."

#3629. Amber Glenn Reacts to 'DWTS' Fans Defending Her After Being Underscored

Amber Glenn is grateful for fans’ support amid her journey on Dancing With the Stars.

“I mean, fans, they’ve got my back,” the Olympic figure skater, 27, exclusively told Us on Tuesday, November 17, after landing in the season 35 finale with pro dance partner Pasha Pashkov.

For weeks, some fans have argued that Glenn and Pashkov, 40, have been underscored by the judges.

“I love you guys. You are ready to fight for me, and I appreciate it,” the gold medalist told her supporters. “I’m your scout leader. We’re gonna go, we’re gonna fight, and you’re gonna fight for me to win because I want us to get that trophy at any cost. Thank you, guys, and we’re going to try our best.”

During the semifinals on Tuesday night, Glenn and Pashkov danced a salsa to “Bemba Colorá” by Celia Cruz and a Viennese waltz to “Dangerous Woman” by Ariana Grande. The pair received all 10s from judges Carrie Ann Inaba, Derek Hough and Bruno Tonioli after both performances, resulting in a total of 60 out of 60 points for the night.

Tuesday’s episode marked the first time that Glenn and Pashkov received perfect scores, which many viewers believe was a long time coming due to the pair’s improvement throughout the season.

“It’s really amazing to have the hard work and dedication acknowledged by the judges,” Glenn told Us on Tuesday. “Their comments really hit home for me. I have been putting in so much work, and Pasha always puts in his 100 percent. So to be able to get that kind of feedback and that result has been incredible.”

The athlete encouraged fans at home to continue voting for her in the finale next week.

“The fans at home [are] keeping things going, keeping things alive, voting. Thank you so much. We’re almost there. Please take us all the way,” she said.

Pashkov gushed over his partner, adding, “She’s the most deserving. She put herself out there, fully, 100 percent vulnerable, every week, diving into every single style, trying to understand its essence through thick and thin. … Fighting through any pain or anything, any doubts, and leaving your heart on the floor every single week. So thank you for doing that, and that is why [fans should vote for her].”

Glenn also reflected on Pashkov’s leadership and revealed what she’s learned from him this season.

“I think something that I noticed, especially from day one, is how you put yourself into something, like, 100 percent,” she told him. “And I think for a long time, I’ve always been scared to because I have a fear of failure. Shocker. And for a long time, that was kind of something I struggled with, was really just putting my all into something out of fear of messing up or failure or something. And he does every — literally every single run, like, gives everything. I’m kind of like, ‘Whoa, what? Like, we’re not performing now. Like, chill out.’ And I’m like, ‘Damn.’”

Glenn continued, “But that’s what makes you such a great competitor and such a great performer, is having that love and dedication and just, like, passion. And that’s something I want to bring into my skating in the future because I felt like I did that tonight. I felt like I was able to give 100 percent, and everything went away, and there wasn’t any fear. There was just love, and there was just emotion and excitement.”

The Dancing With the Stars season 35 finale airs Tuesday, November 24, at 8 p.m. ET on Disney+.

#3627. Yes, You Can Keep Playing GTA 6 After The Credits Roll And Don’t Worry, That’s Not A Spoiler

Grand Theft Auto 6 is a very, very big game with tons of main missions, side missions, activities, random events, races, and more to find and complete. So you might feel compelled to clear out the map before reaching the finale. But you don’t need to do that.

In past Rockstar Games, like GTA V and Red Dead Redemption 2, the studio has let players return to the open world after finishing the main story. However, how this has been handled has varied. In RDR2, you take on the role of another character who can complete activities and side missions after the credits roll. In GTA IV, the game just lets you keep playing post-credits as Niko. This is how it works in most GTA games, actually. Things are a bit different in GTA 6.

Instead, before you enter the final mission, which took me about 90 hours or so to reach in my playthrough, the game makes a big point of asking if you want to go forward with the finale or not. Once you wrap up that big, multi-mission finale and see one of the game’s main endings, GTA 6 tosses you back in time to that moment when you were asked if you wanted to finish the story or not. But this time, Jason and Lucia say no; they aren’t ready, and head back out into Vice City. At that point, you can keep playing GTA 6, wrap up everything on the map, and explore. (The finale mission marker remains on the map if you want to finish the game again and possibly get a different ending.)

It’s an interesting way to handle the endgame and is unlike any past Grand Theft Auto. It also lets GTA 6‘s ending go in a lot of different directions, depending on your choices. I’m not going to even hint at what those endings are, but I’ve seen two of them and trust me, they play out in wildly different and sometimes surprising ways.

The one downside to this approach is that GTA 6 feels a bit frozen in time at the end of the game. No new major storylines can be introduced, as they would possibly get in the way of the narrative wrapping up.

But hey, once you beat the final mission, you unlock the ability to reach 100 percent completion and even unlock the ability to complete challenges to reveal in-game cheat codes that let you go wild in Vice City. So consider it a vacation for Jason and Lucia after all your hard work as a criminal.

I'd love to see these characters back aboard the Black Pearl.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Johnny Depp returning to theaters in Ebenezer on the 2026 movie schedule, renewed interest has grown in whether he'll ever play Captain Jack Sparrow again. Producer Jerry Bruckheimer has already confirmed that discussions have taken place about bringing Depp back for Pirates of the Caribbean 6, although nothing has been officially announced. Now another familiar face from the original movies has weighed in, and I have to admit, this is one reunion I'd love to see happen.

Mackenzie Crook, who played the perpetually confused Ragetti in the first three Pirates movies, recently discussed the possibility of returning to the franchise during an appearance on The Daily Beast's Obsessed podcast. The actor, who starred alongside Lee Arenberg's Pintel as one of the series' most entertaining comedic duos, hasn't appeared in a Pirates movie since 2007's At World's End. Although nearly 20 years later, he sounds more than willing to dig out that wooden eye. Crook explained:

Yes, I think I would for the hell of it. It would be so interesting – obviously it would depend on the script – to even just have a cameo to see what happened to those characters, Pintel and Ragetti, what happened to them after we last saw them. Again, I was really fond of those characters and working with Lee Arenberg, who plays Pintel. Yeah, we had a blast doing that stuff. It was great.

I would absolutely love this. Pintel and Ragetti were two of my favorite supporting characters from the original trilogy, and their ridiculous behavior provided some great comic relief between all the sword fights and increasingly more extravagant set pieces.

For anybody who needs a refresher, the pair started as members of Barbossa's cursed crew in The Curse of the Black Pearl. Ragetti was the skinny, somewhat dimwitted pirate with a wooden eye. Pintel was his considerably louder and equally incompetent partner.

Somehow, they survived three movies filled with undead pirates, sea monsters and increasingly complicated betrayals. That's honestly impressive considering how frequently they seemed to have no idea what was going on. While I certainly want to see Johnny Depp return as Jack Sparrow, I think bringing back characters like these could be just as important to making another Pirates movie feel connected to the originals.

Crook also had some interesting memories of working on the films. During the interview, he recalled the sometimes exhausting experience of shooting aboard actual ships at sea. He also discussed the rather uncomfortable process of bringing Ragetti's wooden eye to life, which required wearing two contact lenses, including one designed to create the appearance of wood grain.

Apparently, playing a pirate wasn't quite as glamorous as it looked. The actor also reflected on the amount of practical filmmaking involved in the original trilogy. Although the movies relied heavily on visual effects, Crook remembered productions where crews actually rigged ships with explosives rather than recreating everything digitally. He described those experiences as some of the last examples of old-fashioned blockbuster filmmaking.

I think that's part of what makes those first three movies so much fun to revisit with a Disney+ subscription. Even when the stories got complicated, something fantastically chaotic about watching these characters run around enormous pirate ships, usually making whatever situation they were in considerably worse. Of course, whether any of them actually return is another matter.

Bruckheimer previously confirmed that he's been speaking with Depp about a sixth movie, although the project remains in development. Depp recently suggested he'd be interested in helping give the franchise a proper sendoff, particularly if it meant working with Bruckheimer again.

Meanwhile, other original cast members have expressed interest in returning. Orlando Bloom has discussed the possibility of another Pirates movie, though there's still no indication that Will Turner will be part of whatever Disney ultimately decides to make.

That's really where we stand. There's no confirmed cast or release date for Pirates of the Caribbean 6, and Crook's comments are just an expression of interest, not evidence he's been approached.

I do like his idea of a cameo that lets audiences catch up with Pintel and Ragetti. It's been almost two decades since we last saw the two idiots, and I can't help wondering what they've been doing with themselves.
